conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting, just a way to see how your mood and anxiety are doing so we can best support you. Everything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and you can pause or stop at any time. Ready for the first one?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute video or if the baby does something silly, but it feels forced—like I’m going through the motions. Nothing really feels funny inside anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I haven’t. I might give a little chuckle if my husband makes a joke, but it fades fast and I don’t feel it—like I’m just pretending.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—grabbing coffee with a friend or even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I’ll think “I should want this,” but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way more than I’d like to admit. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right. Spit-up on the couch? Must be my fault for not burping him long enough. I know in my head that babies cry and messes happen, but I still hear this little voice saying I’m failing at the one job I’m supposed to be good at.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not getting enough milk, or I’ll lie down and picture her crib blanket somehow smothering her. Nothing sets it off—my mind just jumps to the worst-case scenario and won’t let go.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—at least a few times this week. I’ll be folding laundry while she naps and out of nowhere my chest gets tight and it feels like I can’t breathe. There’s no real danger, but in that moment I’m convinced something awful is about to happen to the baby or to me, and I just have to pace the hallway until it passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Even little stuff—like sterilizing the bottles or answering a text—feels like one more brick on a pile that’s already too high. I keep telling myself I just need to push through, but by evening I’m so drained I want to sit in the dark and not move.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah. I’ll lie down exhausted, but then my head starts spinning—replaying every tiny thing I might’ve done wrong, worrying something will happen to the baby if I fall asleep. Some nights I’m still awake when my husband’s alarm goes off. I maybe catch a few broken hours in the early morning, but it never feels like real rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, yeah. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding the baby and suddenly feel tears coming for no real reason. I try to tell myself I should be happy—she’s healthy, we’re safe—but the sadness just sits there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… a few times this week. Sometimes it’s because I feel overwhelmed, but other times the tears just show up—like I’ll be rocking her at 3 a.m. and start sobbing quietly so I won’t wake her. It feels like the sadness leaks out whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better for her.

You've shared that since your baby arrived you feel persistently low, anxious, and overwhelmed. You describe a heavy cloud of sadness, nightly insomnia, and frequent tears, yet you still summon energy to care for your infant while feeling you're somehow failing. Your worries about the baby's safety pop up without warning, and even simple tasks feel like bricks on an already towering pile. Laughing and looking forward to things now feel forced or absent, and you're exhausted by the constant self-blame and panic that arrive uninvited.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no genuine laughter and feeling forced; this aligns with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, self-critical thoughts triggered by routine infant care, indicating self-blame occurs "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive worst-case-scenario thoughts without triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes being overwhelmed "most of the time" by even small tasks, matching the highest-severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-nightly insomnia driven by distressing ruminations, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by overwhelm and spontaneous nightly sobbing, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 25/30 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and meets <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> through five depressive symptoms present most days: depressed mood, markedly diminished interest, guilt, insomnia, and impaired functioning. High scores on anxiety items also suggest comorbid perinatal <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Begin evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> if recommended
3. Plan daily 15-minute support blocks-accept help with feeds/housework so you can nap, shower, or simply rest
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises during panic spikes; keep lights low and audio distraction ready for night feedings
5. Connect with local or online <med>postpartum support groups</med> (e.g., Postpartum Support International) to reduce isolation and normalize recovery
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress and adjust interventions
7. If thoughts of self-harm ever emerge, treat as an emergency: contact 988, your provider, or go to the nearest emergency department
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant approx. 3–4 wks old (per narrative)  
Date: ___

Symptoms endorsed (≥ 7/10 items positive):
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, inability to feel joy; laughs only fleetingly and “feels like pretending.”
- Marked anhedonia: no anticipation of enjoyment in previously pleasant activities.
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“failing at the one job I’m supposed to be good at”).
- Daily free-floating anxiety, catastrophic worries about infant safety; heart racing without trigger.
- Multiple panic-like episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness, pacing) this week.
- Overwhelmed by routine tasks; describes “bricks on a pile already too high.”
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by ruminations and safety fears.
- Frequent crying spells, sometimes spontaneous while caring for baby.

Safety: Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10 negative). No suicidal ideation voiced.

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” causing functional impairment (household tasks, social withdrawal, daytime exhaustion).

Risk indicators: High congruence with perinatal depression and comorbid anxiety; insomnia tied to mood; no protective enjoyment or respite; infant-focused guilt/safety worries.

Plan: Continue screening / refer for comprehensive perinatal mental health evaluation; monitor safety at every contact.
